description: For the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, we want to turn complex lunar mission data into a clear, interactive experience where users can explore landing sites, understand sunlight and Earth visibility, examine communication opportunities, compare locations, and investigate mission windows. Currently starting as a solo-led project and open to a small number of strong collaborators.
summary:
Moonline is a web-based lunar mission-planning aid that compares candidate landing regions by how the Sun and Earth appear from a chosen lunar location over time. Users select a site on an interactive NASA Moon Trek map, or enter coordinates, and choose a UTC time window. Moonline then retrieves Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation from NASA JPL Horizons for a lunar surface observer and identifies when each is geometrically above the horizon. Up to three sites can be compared under identical settings, and results can be exported as traceable reports.

This addresses the challenge of evaluating landing sites by solar illumination and Earth visibility. Sun visibility informs power and thermal planning, while Earth visibility informs communications. Moonline makes this early-stage screening transparent: every result records its data source, reference frame, time scale and method, and missing data is never treated as zero. It also states its limits clearly, and does not claim terrain clearance, power sufficiency, link availability or landing safety.
details:
What it does and how it works

Moonline lets a user explore the lunar surface on an interactive map built from NASA Moon Trek WMTS tiles (global and south-polar imagery, LOLA relief and polar overlays), rendered with OpenLayers using the correct lunar projections. Users can select up to three candidate sites by clicking the map, searching NASA lunar feature names, or typing coordinates. They then choose a UTC start time, an analysis window (1, 7, 14 or 30 days) and a sampling step.

For each site, a Next.js server route requests Sun and Earth observer tables from NASA JPL Horizons, using a Moon-centred lunar surface observer with geodetic coordinates and airless apparent positions. The server validates the returned metadata (centre body, target, reference frame, lunar figure and UTC sample times) before using any angles. It then derives the Sun's and Earth's azimuth and elevation, identifies when each is geometrically above the ideal horizon, and interpolates horizon crossings between samples. The results are shown as an elevation timeline with visibility windows, and as Markdown reports that include all inputs, provenance and any failed targets or sites.

Benefits

  • Early-stage landing-site screening based on Sun visibility (power and thermal planning) and Earth visibility (communications).
  • Side-by-side comparison of up to three sites under identical settings.
  • Full traceability: each result records its source, reference frame, time scale, method and retrieval time.
  • Shareable and restorable sessions through validated URL state.
  • Accessible results: the timeline has text and table alternatives, and manual coordinate entry works even if the map imagery is unavailable.

Intended impact

Moonline aims to make lunar site-visibility analysis easier to understand and verify for students, researchers and mission-planning enthusiasts, using NASA's free and open data. Its longer-term goal is a foundation for terrain-adjusted visibility, using LOLA elevation data, and for a verified map-to-observer frame transformation.

Tools and technologies

Next.js (App Router), TypeScript (strict mode), Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui with Radix UI, Lucide icons, OpenLayers, Apache ECharts, Playwright for browser testing, pnpm, and Vercel for hosting. Data sources: NASA JPL Horizons, NASA Moon Trek (WMTS tiles and nomenclature service). No special hardware was required.

Creativity

Rather than producing an attractive but unverified dashboard, Moonline treats scientific honesty as the core feature. It keeps four ideas strictly separate: astronomical position, geometric visibility, terrain-adjusted visibility and operational suitability. It deliberately avoids an arbitrary overall site score. Missing data appears as gaps, never as zero or "not visible". It also presents the Sun and Earth on one timeline across multiple sites, which makes trade-offs between candidates visible at a glance.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific correctness: coordinate conventions, reference frames, time scales and longitude direction were verified instead of assumed.
  • Validation: tests use archived real NASA/JPL responses as reference cases, and the application never substitutes fabricated data when a provider fails.
  • Limits: we considered what the app must not claim (terrain clearance, power sufficiency, link reliability, landing safety) and state them in the interface and on a Methodology page.
  • Reliability: bounded request sizes and date ranges, timeouts, and clear loading, empty and error states.
  • Accessibility and responsiveness: keyboard navigation, focus handling and layouts tested at mobile, tablet and desktop widths.
